questions.prompt: Which assertion fails a sample when it takes longer than a set number of milliseconds?
questions.explanation: The Duration Assertion checks elapsed time. Size checks bytes, Response checks text/codes and JSON Assertion checks JSON paths/values.

questions.prompt: In a JSON Extractor, what is `$.user.id`?
options: A JSONPath expression selecting the id field inside user
questions.explanation: JSON Extractor uses JSONPath; $ is the root. Regex, XPath and functions use different syntax.

questions.prompt: A Regular Expression Extractor's 'Default Value' is assigned when the expression does not match.
questions.explanation: Setting a clear default like NOT_FOUND makes failed extractions obvious in later requests.

questions.prompt: A Regular Expression Extractor runs on this body with Name `item`, expression `id=(\d+)`, template `$1$`, Match No. -1. Which variables exist afterwards?
questions.explanation: Match No. -1 returns all matches as name_1..name_N plus name_matchNr. Numbering starts at 1.

questions.prompt: A Response Assertion uses pattern matching rule 'Contains' with pattern `Order (\d+) created`. What kind of pattern is that?
options: A regular expression (Contains and Matches use regex; Substring and Equals are literal)
questions.explanation: In Response Assertion, Contains and Matches treat patterns as regular expressions; Substring and Equals are plain text. So special characters like ( need escaping when you mean them literally.

questions.prompt: Which are good assertion practices under load? Select all that apply.
options: Check a business-level marker in the body, not just the status code
Prefer cheap assertions (Response, JSON, Duration) over heavy ones like XML Schema on every sample
Assert on every byte of large responses with Compare Assertion
Use 'Not' to check an error text is absent
questions.explanation: Meaningful, cheap checks keep both correctness and generator capacity. Compare Assertion stores and compares full responses and is not suited to load.

questions.prompt: A JSON Extractor with path `$.items[*].id` and Match No. 1 sets `itemId` correctly in GUI tests but sometimes `NOT_FOUND` under load. The JTL shows those samples returned 200 with body `{"items":[]}`. What is the right action?
options: Add an assertion that items is not empty so the sample fails visibly, then investigate why the API returns empty results under load
Switch to a Regular Expression Extractor
questions.explanation: The extractor is correct; the data is empty. Asserting it turns silent bad data into an error you can count and investigate. Random match, regex or heap changes do not create items.

questions.prompt: You must check that the `total` field equals the sum of line prices in each order response. Which element fits best?
options: A JSR223 Assertion in Groovy that parses the JSON and compares the values, setting AssertionResult failure with a message
questions.explanation: Cross-field logic needs code. A JSR223 Assertion can compute and fail with a clear message. The other assertions check fixed text, time or size only.

coding.title: Emulate the Regular Expression Extractor
coding.prompt:
Write `regex_extract(body, name, regex, template, match_no, default)` returning a dict of JMeter variables:

- `template` uses `$1$`, `$2$` for groups (e.g. `'$2$-$1$'`).
- `match_no` 1..n picks that match; if it does not exist set `{name: default}`.
- `match_no` -1: return `{name+'_1': ..., ..., name+'_matchNr': str(count)}` (no plain `name`). With no matches, return `{name: default, name+'_matchNr': '0'}`.

Example: `regex_extract('id=4&type=book', 'v', r'id=(\d+)&type=(\w+)', '$2$', 1, 'NF')` returns `{'v': 'book'}`.
coding.explanation: `re.finditer` finds every match; the template is filled by replacing each `$n$` with group n. Match No. -1 produces the numbered variables a ForEach Controller loops over.
hints: Number -1 results from 1 with `enumerate(matches, 1)` and add `_matchNr`.

tests.name: All matches
tests.code:
r = regex_extract('id=11 id=22 id=33', 'item', r'id=(\d+)', '$1$', -1, 'NF')
assert r == {'item_1':'11','item_2':'22','item_3':'33','item_matchNr':'3'}, r

tests.name: Default when missing
tests.code:
assert regex_extract('nothing', 'v', r'id=(\d+)', '$1$', 1, 'NF') == {'v': 'NF'}
assert regex_extract('id=1', 'v', r'id=(\d+)', '$1$', 2, 'NF') == {'v': 'NF'}

coding.title: A Response Assertion evaluator
coding.prompt:
Write `response_assertion(text, rule, patterns, negate=False)` returning `True` if the assertion passes. Rules (all patterns must satisfy the rule):

- `'substring'`: literal `p in text`
- `'equals'`: `text == p`
- `'contains'`: regex `re.search(p, text)`
- `'matches'`: regex `re.fullmatch(p, text)`

With `negate=True`, each check is inverted (the pattern must NOT satisfy the rule).

Example: `response_assertion('Order 42 created', 'contains', [r'Order \d+ created'])` is `True`.
coding.explanation: The four rules differ in two ways: literal versus regex, and partial versus whole-text. `check(p) != negate` flips the result when Not is ticked.
hints: Write a helper that evaluates one pattern for the rule.

tests.name: Regex contains
tests.code:
assert response_assertion('Order 42 created', 'contains', [r'Order \d+ created']) is True
assert response_assertion('Order x created', 'contains', [r'Order \d+ created']) is False

tests.name: Substring is literal
tests.code:
assert response_assertion('a(b)', 'substring', ['(b)']) is True
assert response_assertion('ab', 'substring', ['a.']) is False

tests.name: Matches whole text
tests.code: assert response_assertion('OK', 'matches', ['O.']) is True and response_assertion('OK!', 'matches', ['O.']) is False

tests.name: Not
tests.code:
assert response_assertion('{"error":null}', 'substring', ['timeout'], negate=True) is True
assert response_assertion('error: timeout', 'substring', ['timeout'], negate=True) is False

coding.title: A tiny JSONPath for extractors
coding.prompt:
Write `json_path(obj, path)` supporting paths like `$.a.b`, `$.items[0].id` and `$.items[*].id`. Return a **list** of matched values (empty list if nothing matches; never raise for missing keys or out-of-range indexes).

Example: `json_path({'items':[{'id':1},{'id':2}]}, '$.items[*].id')` returns `[1, 2]`.
coding.explanation: Tokenise the path, then carry a list of current nodes forward: keys select from dicts, indexes from lists, and `*` fans out. Missing pieces just drop out, which is why an extractor falls back to its default value instead of crashing.
hints: Tokenise with a regex that matches `.name` or `[n]`/`[*]`.
Keep a list of current nodes; each token maps it to the next list.
Check types and bounds so missing parts give an empty list.
